title: Chemistry Practical II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L organic/general chemistry laboratory curriculum, complementing CHM209 (volumetric/quantitative practical): laboratory safety, purification techniques (recrystallization, distillation, sublimation), determination of physical constants (melting/boiling point, refractive index, density), solvent extraction, qualitative organic functional-group tests, and basic chromatography.

questions.question: Before starting any practical involving flammable organic solvents, the FIRST safety precaution a student should take is to:
options: Ensure there are no naked flames nearby and work in a well-ventilated area or fume cupboard
Wear only gloves, since flames are not a concern with organic solvents
Store all solvents next to the Bunsen burner for convenience
Taste a small amount of the solvent to identify it
questions.correct_answer: Ensure there are no naked flames nearby and work in a well-ventilated area or fume cupboard
questions.explanation: Many organic solvents are volatile and flammable, so naked flames must be eliminated and vapours ventilated away before handling them, to prevent fire or inhalation hazards.

questions.question: Recrystallization is used to purify a solid organic compound because it relies on the principle that:
options: The compound and its impurities have identical solubility in all solvents
The compound's solubility in a solvent increases with temperature, so it dissolves hot and crystallizes out as pure solid on cooling while impurities stay in solution
The impurities evaporate completely on heating
The solid sublimes directly from solid to vapour
questions.correct_answer: The compound's solubility in a solvent increases with temperature, so it dissolves hot and crystallizes out as pure solid on cooling while impurities stay in solution
questions.explanation: A suitable recrystallization solvent dissolves much more solute hot than cold; on cooling a saturated hot solution, pure crystals separate first while small amounts of impurity remain dissolved in the mother liquor.

questions.question: An ideal recrystallization solvent for a given solid should:
options: Dissolve the compound readily when cold and remain insoluble when hot
Dissolve the compound well when hot but only sparingly when cold, and not react with the compound
React chemically with the compound to form a new soluble derivative
Have the same boiling point as the compound's melting point
questions.correct_answer: Dissolve the compound well when hot but only sparingly when cold, and not react with the compound
questions.explanation: A good recrystallization solvent shows a large difference in solubility between hot and cold conditions and is chemically inert towards the solute, maximizing recovery of pure crystals on cooling.

questions.question: During recrystallization, activated charcoal (decolourizing carbon) is added to the hot solution mainly to:
options: Adsorb coloured impurities and resinous materials from the solution
Increase the solubility of the desired compound
Lower the boiling point of the solvent
Act as a nucleation site for excess crystal growth only
questions.correct_answer: Adsorb coloured impurities and resinous materials from the solution
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal has a very large surface area and adsorbs coloured or resinous impurities from the hot solution, which are then removed together with the charcoal during hot filtration.

questions.question: Hot filtration is carried out immediately after adding decolourizing charcoal in a recrystallization mainly to prevent:
options: The solution from boiling over
Premature crystallization of the product in the funnel or filter paper as the solution cools
Loss of solvent by evaporation
The charcoal from dissolving in the solvent
questions.correct_answer: Premature crystallization of the product in the funnel or filter paper as the solution cools
questions.explanation: If the saturated solution is allowed to cool before filtering, crystals form and clog the filter paper/funnel and are lost with the charcoal, so filtration is done quickly while the solution is still hot.

questions.question: The melting point of a pure organic solid is generally characterised by:
options: A wide melting range of more than 10 degC
A sharp, narrow melting range (typically within 1-2 degC)
No definite melting point at all
A melting point that decreases as more impurity is added
questions.correct_answer: A sharp, narrow melting range (typically within 1-2 degC)
questions.explanation: Pure crystalline solids melt sharply over a narrow temperature range; the presence of impurities broadens and typically lowers the melting range, which is used as a purity criterion.

questions.question: A 'mixed melting point' determination, in which a small sample of a known compound is mixed with an unknown and the melting point taken, is used to:
options: Raise the melting point of the unknown artificially
Confirm the identity of the unknown: if the mixture melts sharply at the same temperature as the pure components, they are likely the same compound; a depression indicates they differ
Determine the boiling point of the mixture instead
Measure the density of the unknown compound
questions.correct_answer: Confirm the identity of the unknown: if the mixture melts sharply at the same temperature as the pure components, they are likely the same compound; a depression indicates they differ
questions.explanation: Two different compounds act as mutual impurities and depress and broaden each other's melting point when mixed; an undepressed, sharp mixed melting point is strong evidence the two samples are identical.

questions.question: Simple distillation is most appropriate for separating:
options: Two miscible liquids with very close boiling points (differing by less than 5 degC)
A volatile liquid from a non-volatile dissolved solid, or liquids with widely different boiling points (differing by more than about 25 degC)
Two immiscible liquids of similar density
A solid mixture with no liquid phase present
questions.correct_answer: A volatile liquid from a non-volatile dissolved solid, or liquids with widely different boiling points (differing by more than about 25 degC)
questions.explanation: Simple distillation gives only one theoretical plate of separation, so it effectively purifies a volatile liquid from non-volatile solutes or separates liquids whose boiling points differ widely; closer boiling points require fractional distillation.

questions.question: Fractional distillation achieves better separation of liquids with close boiling points than simple distillation because:
options: It uses a much larger flask
The fractionating column provides repeated vaporization-condensation cycles (multiple theoretical plates) that progressively enrich the vapour in the more volatile component
It is always carried out under vacuum
It removes the need for a thermometer
questions.correct_answer: The fractionating column provides repeated vaporization-condensation cycles (multiple theoretical plates) that progressively enrich the vapour in the more volatile component
questions.explanation: Each theoretical plate in a fractionating column represents an equilibrium vaporization-condensation step, so multiple plates progressively concentrate the more volatile component in the vapour reaching the condenser, giving sharper separation than a single simple distillation.

questions.question: Steam distillation is particularly useful for isolating volatile organic compounds (e.g. essential oils) that are:
options: Fully miscible with water and thermally stable at their normal boiling point
Immiscible with water and would decompose if distilled alone at their normal (higher) boiling point
Non-volatile solids only
Highly soluble in water at all temperatures
questions.correct_answer: Immiscible with water and would decompose if distilled alone at their normal (higher) boiling point
questions.explanation: In steam distillation, a water-immiscible compound co-distils with steam below 100 degC (since the mixture boils when the sum of the two partial vapour pressures equals atmospheric pressure), allowing its isolation without thermal decomposition.

questions.question: Vacuum (reduced-pressure) distillation is used mainly to purify liquids that:
options: Boil at very low temperatures already, well below room temperature
Would decompose or oxidise if heated to their normal (atmospheric) boiling point
Are completely non-volatile
Have a boiling point below their melting point
questions.correct_answer: Would decompose or oxidise if heated to their normal (atmospheric) boiling point
questions.explanation: Lowering the external pressure lowers a liquid's boiling point, allowing distillation of thermally sensitive, high-boiling compounds at a much lower temperature, avoiding decomposition.

questions.question: Sublimation, used to purify certain solids (e.g. naphthalene, iodine, benzoic acid), works because the solid:
options: Melts to a liquid and is then filtered
Passes directly from the solid phase to the vapour phase (and back to solid on a cold surface) without going through the liquid phase
Reacts with the container material to form a purified derivative
Dissolves completely in the crucible material
questions.correct_answer: Passes directly from the solid phase to the vapour phase (and back to solid on a cold surface) without going through the liquid phase
questions.explanation: Sublimable solids have an appreciable vapour pressure below their melting point; heating vaporises the solid directly, and the vapour recondenses as purified crystals on a cooler surface, leaving non-volatile impurities behind.

questions.question: In liquid-liquid solvent extraction of an organic compound from an aqueous solution, using several smaller portions of extracting solvent instead of one large portion of the same total volume:
options: Always gives a poorer overall extraction efficiency
Gives a higher overall extraction efficiency, because of the mathematics of the distribution law applied repeatedly
Makes no difference to the amount extracted
Is only relevant when the solvents are miscible
questions.correct_answer: Gives a higher overall extraction efficiency, because of the mathematics of the distribution law applied repeatedly
questions.explanation: Because of the distribution (partition) law, several successive extractions with smaller solvent portions remove more total solute than a single extraction with the same overall solvent volume.

questions.question: In a separating funnel, after shaking an organic solvent with an aqueous solution and allowing the layers to settle, the denser layer is:
options: Always the organic layer regardless of solvent
Run off first from the bottom tap, and its identity (aqueous or organic) is confirmed by testing miscibility of a small portion with water
Always discarded without testing
Left in the funnel while the upper layer is drained through the tap
questions.correct_answer: Run off first from the bottom tap, and its identity (aqueous or organic) is confirmed by testing miscibility of a small portion with water
questions.explanation: The two immiscible layers separate by density with the denser layer at the bottom; since either layer could be denser depending on the solvent used, a small sample is tested for miscibility with water to confirm which layer is aqueous.

questions.question: Anhydrous sodium sulphate or calcium chloride is commonly added to an organic layer after extraction to:
options: Remove coloured impurities
Act as a drying agent, absorbing residual traces of water from the organic solvent
Neutralize any remaining acid
Increase the boiling point of the solvent permanently
questions.correct_answer: Act as a drying agent, absorbing residual traces of water from the organic solvent
questions.explanation: Anhydrous inorganic salts such as sodium sulphate absorb residual water as water of crystallisation, drying the organic layer before further purification steps such as distillation.

questions.question: Bromine water is used as a qualitative test reagent for unsaturation in organic compounds. A positive test for a carbon-carbon double bond is indicated by:
options: No visible change at all
Rapid decolourization of the orange/brown bromine water as it adds across the double bond
Formation of a white precipitate only
Evolution of a colourless gas with a pungent smell
questions.correct_answer: Rapid decolourization of the orange/brown bromine water as it adds across the double bond
questions.explanation: Alkenes and other unsaturated compounds decolourize bromine water rapidly through electrophilic addition of bromine across the double bond, a simple and classic test for unsaturation.

questions.question: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) is used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones because aldehydes give a positive result shown by:
options: Formation of a silver mirror on the inside of the test tube (or a grey/black precipitate) as Ag+ is reduced to metallic silver
A blue-green colour change only
Immediate effervescence of hydrogen gas
Formation of a yellow precipitate of silver iodide
questions.correct_answer: Formation of a silver mirror on the inside of the test tube (or a grey/black precipitate) as Ag+ is reduced to metallic silver
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are readily oxidised and reduce the diamminesilver(I) complex in Tollens' reagent to metallic silver, depositing a characteristic silver mirror, whereas ketones (except alpha-hydroxy ketones) do not react.

questions.question: Fehling's solution, used to test for reducing sugars and aldehydes, gives a positive result shown by:
options: Formation of a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide (Cu2O) on warming
Formation of a deep blue solution that remains unchanged on heating
No colour change under any conditions
Immediate formation of a white precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Formation of a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide (Cu2O) on warming
questions.explanation: In Fehling's test, the blue Cu2+ tartrate complex is reduced by an aldehyde (or reducing sugar) to a brick-red precipitate of Cu2O on warming, which is taken as a positive test.

questions.question: The iodoform test is used to identify compounds containing a methyl ketone group (CH3-CO-) or a secondary alcohol that oxidises to one (CH3-CH(OH)-), and a positive result is shown by:
options: Formation of a pale yellow crystalline precipitate of triiodomethane (iodoform) with a characteristic antiseptic smell
Evolution of a colourless odourless gas
A deep red colouration of the solution
No visible or detectable change
questions.correct_answer: Formation of a pale yellow crystalline precipitate of triiodomethane (iodoform) with a characteristic antiseptic smell
questions.explanation: Iodine and alkali react with methyl ketones (or secondary alcohols oxidisable to them) via haloform reaction to give pale yellow, characteristically smelling iodoform crystals, confirming the CH3CO- group.

questions.question: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP, Brady's reagent) is used to test for the presence of:
options: Carboxylic acids
Aldehydes or ketones (the carbonyl group), giving an orange/yellow precipitate
Alcohols only
Alkyl halides
questions.correct_answer: Aldehydes or ketones (the carbonyl group), giving an orange/yellow precipitate
questions.explanation: 2,4-DNP condenses with the carbonyl carbon of aldehydes and ketones to form an orange/yellow crystalline 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone precipitate, a classic qualitative test for the carbonyl functional group.

questions.question: Litmus paper, universal indicator, or sodium bicarbonate solution can be used to test an unknown organic liquid for the presence of a carboxylic acid because the compound would:
options: Turn blue litmus red, or produce effervescence (CO2 gas) with sodium bicarbonate solution
Have no effect on litmus paper at all
Turn red litmus paper permanently blue
React with sodium bicarbonate to give a precipitate rather than gas
questions.correct_answer: Turn blue litmus red, or produce effervescence (CO2 gas) with sodium bicarbonate solution
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to turn blue litmus red and to liberate CO2 gas (seen as effervescence) from sodium bicarbonate solution, distinguishing them from most other neutral organic functional groups.

questions.question: The ceric ammonium nitrate test is a classical qualitative test used to detect:
options: The presence of a hydroxyl (-OH) group in alcohols, giving a colour change from yellow to red
Only unsaturated hydrocarbons
Only aromatic amines
The presence of halide ions
questions.correct_answer: The presence of a hydroxyl (-OH) group in alcohols, giving a colour change from yellow to red
questions.explanation: Ceric ammonium nitrate reacts with the -OH group of an alcohol to form a red complex, replacing the reagent's original yellow colour, and is used as a specific test for alcohols.

questions.question: In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), spots are best applied to the plate using a fine capillary tube because:
options: A small, concentrated spot gives sharper, more clearly resolved separation than a large, diffuse spot
The spot size has no effect on resolution
Large spots always travel faster up the plate
It prevents the solvent front from moving at all
questions.correct_answer: A small, concentrated spot gives sharper, more clearly resolved separation than a large, diffuse spot
questions.explanation: Applying a small, concentrated spot minimises initial spreading, so the separated components remain as tight, well-resolved spots as the solvent develops the plate, improving accuracy of Rf measurement.

questions.question: In TLC, the baseline (origin) where the sample is spotted must be positioned above the level of the developing solvent in the chamber because:
options: Otherwise the sample would dissolve directly into the bulk solvent reservoir instead of being carried up the plate by capillary action
The solvent level has no bearing on the experiment
It ensures the solvent evaporates faster
It prevents the plate from cracking
questions.correct_answer: Otherwise the sample would dissolve directly into the bulk solvent reservoir instead of being carried up the plate by capillary action
questions.explanation: If the spotted origin is submerged in the solvent reservoir, the sample simply washes off into the bulk solvent rather than being drawn up the plate by capillary action as the solvent front develops.

questions.question: Visualizing colourless spots on a developed TLC plate can be achieved by:
options: Viewing the plate under ultraviolet light (if the plate has a fluorescent indicator) or exposing it to iodine vapour
Adding more developing solvent to the chamber
Heating the plate to exactly 0 degC
There is no method to visualize colourless spots
questions.correct_answer: Viewing the plate under ultraviolet light (if the plate has a fluorescent indicator) or exposing it to iodine vapour
questions.explanation: Many TLC plates contain a fluorescent indicator that is quenched by UV-absorbing spots, and iodine vapour reversibly stains many organic compounds brown, both common ways to visualize otherwise invisible spots.

questions.question: A calibrated pycnometer (density bottle) is used in the laboratory to determine the:
options: Density of a liquid, by comparing the mass of a fixed volume of the liquid with that of the same volume of water
Melting point of a solid
Refractive index of a liquid
Boiling point elevation of a solution
questions.correct_answer: Density of a liquid, by comparing the mass of a fixed volume of the liquid with that of the same volume of water
questions.explanation: A pycnometer has a precisely known fixed volume; weighing it empty, filled with the liquid, and filled with water of known density allows accurate calculation of the liquid's density (or relative density).

questions.question: A refractometer is used in the organic laboratory to measure a liquid's:
options: Refractive index, a physical constant useful for identifying and checking the purity of a liquid
Melting point
Optical rotation of plane-polarised light
Boiling point at reduced pressure
questions.correct_answer: Refractive index, a physical constant useful for identifying and checking the purity of a liquid
questions.explanation: The refractive index (ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the substance) is a precise, reproducible physical constant for a pure liquid and is compared with literature values to check identity and purity.

questions.question: When recording an experimental melting point that is lower and broader than the accepted literature value for a compound, the most likely conclusion is that the sample:
options: Is unusually pure
Contains an impurity, since impurities generally lower and broaden the melting range
Was heated too slowly
Has a higher molecular weight than expected
questions.correct_answer: Contains an impurity, since impurities generally lower and broaden the melting range
questions.explanation: Impurities disrupt the regular crystal lattice, generally lowering the melting point and widening the melting range compared with the pure substance, a principle used to assess purity.

questions.question: In a laboratory report for a purification experiment, the 'percentage yield' of a recrystallized product is calculated as:
options: (Mass of pure product obtained / theoretical or starting mass) x 100%
(Melting point of product / melting point of starting material) x 100%
(Volume of solvent used / mass of product) x 100%
(Mass of solvent recovered / mass of product) x 100%
questions.correct_answer: (Mass of pure product obtained / theoretical or starting mass) x 100%
questions.explanation: Percentage yield expresses the actual mass of purified product recovered as a percentage of the maximum theoretical (or starting) mass, reflecting the efficiency of the purification or reaction.

questions.question: A Liebig condenser is oriented and connected during a distillation so that:
options: Cooling water enters at the bottom (lower) end near the receiver and exits at the top, giving countercurrent flow against the vapour
Cooling water enters at the top and exits at the bottom, flowing in the same direction as the vapour
No water flow is needed if the vapour is cool enough
The condenser is used vertically only, never at an angle
questions.correct_answer: Cooling water enters at the bottom (lower) end near the receiver and exits at the top, giving countercurrent flow against the vapour
questions.explanation: Water is fed in at the lower end (nearer the receiving flask) and drains from the upper end, so it flows counter to the descending vapour/condensate, maximising cooling efficiency along the whole condenser length.

questions.question: Anti-bumping granules (or boiling chips) are added to a flask before distillation or heating a liquid mainly to:
options: Provide nucleation sites for smooth, even boiling and prevent violent, sudden bumping
Increase the boiling point of the liquid
Act as a drying agent for the liquid
Colour the solution for easy identification
questions.correct_answer: Provide nucleation sites for smooth, even boiling and prevent violent, sudden bumping
questions.explanation: Anti-bumping granules have a porous surface that traps air, providing nucleation sites for small, steady bubbles to form, preventing the sudden violent boiling (bumping) that can occur in a superheated liquid.

questions.question: Why must anti-bumping granules never be added to a liquid that is already hot or boiling?
options: They will dissolve instantly and have no effect
The trapped air in the granules is released suddenly, which can cause violent, dangerous frothing or eruption of the hot liquid
They will cool the liquid down too quickly
They react explosively with all organic solvents
questions.correct_answer: The trapped air in the granules is released suddenly, which can cause violent, dangerous frothing or eruption of the hot liquid
questions.explanation: Adding boiling chips to an already-hot liquid causes rapid, uncontrolled release of trapped air as bubbles, which can make the superheated liquid erupt suddenly out of the flask, posing a burn hazard.

questions.question: Filter paper folded into a 'fluted' (fan-pleated) pattern is preferred over a simple cone fold for hot gravity filtration in recrystallization because it:
options: Increases the surface area exposed and speeds up filtration, reducing the time available for premature crystal formation
Makes the filtrate more concentrated
Removes coloured impurities more effectively than charcoal
Is required only for filtering cold solutions
questions.correct_answer: Increases the surface area exposed and speeds up filtration, reducing the time available for premature crystal formation
questions.explanation: Fluting increases the exposed surface area of the filter paper and allows air to pass in as liquid passes out, filtering faster than a simple cone and minimising the chance of the hot solution cooling and crystallizing on the paper.

questions.question: A student wishes to confirm whether an unknown white solid is benzoic acid, and has an authentic sample of benzoic acid available. The most appropriate simple confirmatory test from this practical course is to:
options: Compare colours of the two solids visually only
Determine the melting point of the unknown, the known sample, and a well-mixed sample of both (mixed melting point) and compare results
Dissolve both in water and compare volumes
Weigh both samples and compare their masses
questions.correct_answer: Determine the melting point of the unknown, the known sample, and a well-mixed sample of both (mixed melting point) and compare results
questions.explanation: Comparing the melting point of the unknown with an authentic sample, and confirming with an undepressed mixed melting point, is the classical practical method for confirming the identity of an unknown solid organic compound.

questions.question: A crude solid product obtained from an organic reaction is generally purified in the following typical order:
options: Melting point determination, then recrystallization, then dissolving in hot solvent
Dissolve in a minimum volume of hot solvent, hot-filter (with decolourizing charcoal if needed), cool to crystallize, filter and dry the crystals, then check melting point
Dry the solid first, then dissolve it in cold solvent, then boil it dry
Sublime the solid before dissolving it in any solvent
questions.correct_answer: Dissolve in a minimum volume of hot solvent, hot-filter (with decolourizing charcoal if needed), cool to crystallize, filter and dry the crystals, then check melting point
questions.explanation: The standard recrystallization sequence is: dissolve in the minimum hot solvent, hot-filter off insoluble impurities/charcoal, allow slow cooling for crystal growth, filter and wash the crystals, dry them, and finally confirm purity by melting point.

questions.question: In a laboratory notebook/report, recording the exact mass, volume, and observed physical constants (melting point, boiling point) of a compound immediately after each step is important chiefly because it:
options: Provides an accurate, verifiable record for calculating percentage yield and purity, and for reproducing or troubleshooting the experiment later
Reduces the total time needed for the experiment
Is only required if the experiment fails
Replaces the need for any safety precautions
questions.correct_answer: Provides an accurate, verifiable record for calculating percentage yield and purity, and for reproducing or troubleshooting the experiment later
questions.explanation: Contemporaneous, accurate recording of masses, volumes, and physical constants allows correct calculation of yield and purity and gives a reliable record for reproducing the experiment or diagnosing what went wrong.
